headline: The Gulf war reached Saudi oil country overnight and pushed crude back up, just as tech earnings had lifted stocks to within a whisker of records.
dateline: Thursday, October 22, 2026 · closes as of Wed Oct 21

rundown.h: Meta topped forecasts and kept spending like a hyperscaler.
rundown.p: Meta's third-quarter revenue rose 26% to $64.6 billion, ahead of the $63.3 billion expected, and it guided fourth-quarter sales to $73–76 billion. Capex hit $34.9 billion, up from $19.4 billion a year ago, pushing free cash flow to −$2.1 billion, and the 2026 capex range is now $135–145 billion. Shares rose as much as 5% after hours.

rundown.h: Tesla's margins improved, but profit still shrank.
rundown.p: Tesla's revenue was flat at $28.05 billion and adjusted earnings of $0.48 a share edged past the $0.45 consensus, while GAAP net income fell 43% to $787 million. Auto gross margin excluding credits climbed to 18.1% from 15.4% a year ago, and free cash flow swung back to $1.53 billion. Shares slipped about 2% after hours.

rundown.h: AT&T sank 6% as satellites crash the wireless party.
rundown.p: AT&T added 379,000 postpaid phone customers in the third quarter, just shy of the roughly 387,000 analysts expected, and the stock fell about 6% Wednesday. Investors are weighing the threat of satellite-to-phone service from Starlink; CEO John Stankey said such a shift won't happen overnight. For income investors, telecom's reputation as a steady, defensive yield play is getting tested.

rundown.h: Super Micro's forecast jump revived the AI trade.
rundown.p: Super Micro raised its fiscal first-quarter revenue forecast to $18.5–19.5 billion from $14.5–15.5 billion, and its shares jumped as much as 12% Wednesday. The guide signals AI server demand is still running hotter than planned, helping chip and hardware stocks lead the market. It also lands a day after worries about how heavily the AI build-out leans on debt.

rundown.h: Washington offered to lend heating oil to cool diesel.
rundown.p: The administration offered to lend up to about 315,000 barrels, nearly a third of the 1-million-barrel Northeast heating-oil reserve, to help cap diesel prices. It's a small amount next to national demand, but it signals the White House is reaching for policy tools as fuel costs feed inflation. For truckers and shippers, fuel surcharges remain the line item to watch heading into winter.
rundown.src: Reuters via Global Banking & Finance · Oct 22

dive.title: The bond market is still buying. It just wants to be paid.
dive.dek: Treasury auctions keep clearing with healthy demand, but at yields well above 5%, as the term premium hits levels last seen in 2010.
dive.body:
Every few weeks the Treasury tests how much appetite investors still have for its debt, and lately the answer has been: plenty, at the right price. On Oct. 7 a $39 billion 10-year note sale drew bids worth 2.77 times the amount offered, and primary dealers were left holding less than $1 billion. Strong on paper, but it cleared at 5.30%, almost half a point above September's 4.83%. The next day the 30-year sold at 5.618%, up from 5.308% a month earlier, and Wednesday's 20-year reopening cleared at 5.469%, above the prior 5.420%. In late September the 7-year sold at 5.085%, a record high for that auction going back to 2009.

So this isn't a buyers' strike; it's a repricing. The clearest sign is the term premium, the extra yield investors demand to lock money up in long bonds instead of rolling short-term bills. On the Fed's Kim-Wright model it reached about 1.10% on Oct. 5, the highest since April 2010, versus roughly 0.43% a year earlier. It eased to about 0.99% by Oct. 16, still more than double last year's level.

The fiscal math explains a lot of it. The FY2026 deficit came in at $2.0 trillion, or 6.2% of GDP, up from $1.8 trillion, and $115 billion of the $218 billion increase came from higher interest costs alone. Tariffs didn't fill the hole as hoped: customs receipts fell 11% after about $130 billion of court-ordered IEEPA refunds went back to importers. Add inflation running hot and a Fed that hiked in September, and long-bond buyers want more cushion.

The key point for investors: the term premium doesn't fall just because the Fed eventually cuts. It falls when supply or inflation worries ease. That matters for everything priced off the 10-year, from mortgages to industrial cap rates to refinancing costs. If Treasury signals bigger coupon auctions at its November refunding, expect the premium to climb again; a steady-size message and calmer inflation data would be the first real relief.

items.title: September retail sales rose 0.8%, with gasoline doing most of the lifting

chart.src: Source: Census via FRED (RSAFS, current vintage; % change computed).

items.body:
Retail sales rose 0.8% in September, well above the 0.3% consensus, after an upwardly revised 1.3% gain in August. Sales were up 6.3% from a year earlier, versus 5.6% the month before. The figures are not adjusted for inflation, and consumer prices rose 3.7% over the year to September.

Gasoline stations drove the beat: their sales jumped 6.4% as pump prices rose about 7% in the month. Excluding gas stations, sales rose just 0.2% after 1.0% in August, and the control group that feeds into GDP rose 0.1% against 0.3% expected. Furniture stores (+1.3%) and restaurants and bars (+1.1%) gained, while building materials (−0.6%) and miscellaneous stores (−3.0%) fell.

Over the past year, monthly gains have swung widely, from −1.43% (May 2025) to +1.66% (March 2026). The Fed's latest Beige Book said most districts saw little or no change in overall consumer spending.

experts.who: Michael Pearce, chief U.S. economist, Oxford Economics
experts.view: The headline jump was almost all higher gas prices, though third-quarter spending still looks on track for about 3.3% annualized growth before slowing into the holidays.

experts.who: Natalie Kotlyar, retail and consumer products leader, BDO
experts.view: The report shouldn't be read as broad consumer strength, since part of the gain is higher prices and shoppers are leaning on savings and promotions.

items.lean: Both economists quoted read the beat as mostly fuel prices; Oxford still sees solid Q3 spending.
items.src: Sources: Trading Economics (retail sales, Oct 15); Reuters via Yahoo Finance (Oct 15); AP via KSAT (Oct 15); FRED RSAFS.

lead.title: The war reaches Saudi oil country, and the U.S. pulls staff out
lead.body:
The Gulf conflict spread onto Saudi soil overnight. Late Oct 21, Saudi Arabia's energy ministry said debris from a drone intercepted on its way to Aramco's Shaybah oilfield killed two people; oilfield operations were not affected and the ministry didn't name the attacker. The Saudi-led coalition said it downed six drones over the Eastern Province and Medina, while the Houthis denied striking deep inside the kingdom. Early Oct 22, an attack on King Fahd International Airport in Dammam killed one resident and injured eight.

The State Department ordered non-emergency staff and families to leave Saudi Arabia, saying reports of wider Gulf departures were inaccurate. Near Hormuz, the IRGC said three vessels hit mines west of the strait, and Treasury added shadow-fleet shipping agents and vessels to its Iran sanctions.
lead.reach: Through oil and diesel. Brent touched $112.55 on Oct 22, its highest since May 18, and traded at $112.17 (+3.1%) at 0818 GMT, while Kpler said Middle East oil exports are back above 24 million barrels a day, above pre-war levels.

views.view: De-escalation talk lacks credibility while ships and Saudi targets keep getting hit, and he expects no easing before the U.S. midterms.
views.src: Reuters via Global Banking & Finance · Oct 22

views.view: Gulf crude is still getting out: regional exports have recovered past pre-war volumes, though the IEA flags higher freight and insurance costs.

reading.title: The $25 book that sells for thousands
reading.dek: Seth Klarman's out-of-print Margin of Safety argues that avoiding losses comes first, a lesson that bites harder with stocks near records and safe yields above 4%.
body: In 1991, Seth Klarman published his first and only book, Margin of Safety: Risk-Averse Value Investing Strategies for the Thoughtful Investor. It had a cover price of about $25 and went out of print after selling roughly 5,000 copies. Since then, used copies have changed hands for hundreds and sometimes thousands of dollars, which may make it the most expensive investing manual most investors have never read. The subtitle states the priorities plainly: avoid losses first, then look for gains.

Klarman was born in New York City in 1957. He studied economics at Cornell, graduating in 1979, and then earned an MBA at Harvard Business School as a Baker Scholar. In 1982 he helped launch The Baupost Group with a small circle of backers, starting from $27 million. When Baupost opened to new investors in 2008, it raised $4 billion. The firm later grew to manage roughly $30 billion.

The book's central idea comes from Benjamin Graham and David Dodd, who introduced the phrase margin of safety in 1934. Klarman's version starts from humility. Business value is a range, not a precise number, and analysts make mistakes, so you buy only when the gap between price and value is wide enough to absorb errors and bad luck. He separates investors, who compare a price with what the underlying business is worth, from speculators, who are betting on what the next buyer will pay.

Two of the book's arguments still sit uneasily with much of the industry. The first is that absolute returns matter more than relative ones: if your fund drops 20% while the index drops 25%, you have still lost money. The second is that holding cash is a legitimate choice when bargains are scarce. Waiting in cash beats forcing money into mediocre or overpriced ideas, because markets move in cycles of overreaction in both directions and bargains eventually return.

That makes the book an uncomfortable read today. Stocks sit near records, so the cushion between price and value is thin by definition. With Treasury bills yielding more than 4%, waiting now pays real money, which removes the old excuse that there is no alternative. And with a war in the Gulf moving oil prices day to day, the market is facing exactly the kind of surprise a margin of safety exists to absorb. The book doesn't ask you to predict when the cycle turns. It asks you to be ready, with room for error, when it does.
takeaways: With stocks near records, the gap between price and value is thin. Size accordingly.
Bills above 4% make holding cash for bargains a cheap choice.
A Gulf oil shock is the kind of surprise a margin of safety absorbs.
